nameStory: These tiny fungi earned the name "fairy pins" because they look exactly like miniature black pins or needles that might belong in a fairy's sewing kit. Standing just 2.5mm tall with thin dark stalks topped by slightly wider caps, they really do resemble tiny matchsticks or pins stuck into mushroom surfaces.
description: Fairy pins are microscopic parasitic fungi that look like clusters of tiny black matchsticks growing on other mushrooms. These non-lichenized fungi reach a maximum height of just 2.5 millimeters, making them smaller than most ants! They have thin dark stalks topped with slightly wider caps, and grow in groups or neat rows on the surfaces of their host fungi. You'll need to look very closely or use a magnifying glass to appreciate these miniature marvels.

idTips.label: Tiny matchstick shape
idTips.description: Look for clusters of what appear to be microscopic black matchsticks or pins, each less than 2.5mm tall with thin stalks and slightly wider dark caps

idTips.label: Host mushroom
idTips.description: Growing directly on the caps of shelf fungi, especially the violet-toothed polypore (Trichaptum biforme) or turkey tail mushrooms

idTips.label: Growth pattern
idTips.description: Arranged in orderly groups or rows across the mushroom surface, not scattered randomly

idTips.label: Color and texture
idTips.description: Consistently black or very dark brown with a smooth, pin-like appearance that feels firm to gentle touch

idTips.label: Spore color
idTips.description: Very pale brown spores (visible only with microscope) distinguish them from other pin fungi

idTips.label: Associated algae
idTips.description: Often accompanied by patches of green algae growing on the same host mushroom surface

habitat: Fairy pins are found in New England's deciduous and mixed forests where their host fungi grow on dead hardwood logs and branches. Look for them on shelf fungi growing from fallen trees, dead branches, and decaying wood in moist woodland areas. They're most common in mature forests with plenty of decomposing wood, from lowland areas up to mid-elevation slopes.

seasonality.spring: Fairy pins begin appearing as temperatures warm and moisture increases, establishing on fresh host fungi that have overwintered or newly emerged on decomposing wood.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when fairy pins are most visible and abundant, thriving in the warm, humid conditions that also favor their mushroom hosts.
seasonality.fall: Continue to be present and often quite noticeable as many shelf fungi produce new growth during the cool, moist autumn weather.
seasonality.winter: May persist on their hosts in protected locations, though growth slows significantly in the cold temperatures.

funFact: These tiny fungi are actually pirates of the mushroom world — they're parasites that hijack other fungi's hard work, stealing nutrients from shelf mushrooms that are already busy decomposing dead wood!
confusionNotes: Fairy pins can be confused with other pin fungi in the same genus, but their very pale brown spores (visible only under magnification) and their strong preference for growing on Trichaptum biforme help distinguish them. Remember: if it's on turkey tail or violet-toothed polypore and looks like tiny black pins, it's likely fairy pins.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their common name suggesting something magical, fairy pins are serious decomposers playing an important ecological role. The term "non-lichenized fungus" simply means they don't form partnerships with algae like lichens do, even though algae often grow nearby on the same surfaces.
compareHints: Fairy pins can be distinguished from their close relative, poplar needles (Phaeocalicium populneum), primarily by their host preference and spore color. While both look like tiny black pins, fairy pins specifically target shelf fungi like Trichaptum biforme and have very pale brown spores, whereas poplar needles typically grow on different substrates. The microscopic spore examination is the most reliable way to separate these nearly identical species.
